To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the opiate receptor labeled with 3H-etorpine in rat-brain membrane preparations is also involved in antagonism by opiate antagonists of acute opiate action in the ileum and in precipitation of a withdrawal response in morphine-dependent animals.
the receptor sites that bind 3H-etorpine are the same receptors involved in the antagonism of acute opioid effects and precipitation of withdrawal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the opiate receptors and the development of opiate antagonistic compounds.
the development of a new class of potent, non-addicting opiate antagonists that are devoid of agonist activity.
the study of the effects of various compounds, both agonists and antagonists, on the binding of 3H-opiates to rat-brain homogenates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the binding site labeled by 3 H-etorphine is the same as the receptor involved in antagonism in the isolated guinea pig ileum and in the precipitated withdrawal in the rhesus monkey.
the binding of opiate agonists and antagonists to opiate receptors is a prerequisite to the manifestation of their effects.

the binding of 3H-opiates to opiate receptors in the brain is related to their ability to antagonize acute opiate effects, and to precipitate withdrawal in morphine dependent animals, but not to precipitate withdrawal when administered to man.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dextroisomers of the antagonists studied were less active in all of these assays than were the levoisomers and that the quaternary compounds were less active than were the corresponding tertiary compounds.
the d-isomers of nalorphine and naltrexone are the most potent opiate antagonists known and are 10-20 times more potent than naloxone.
the receptor binding, in vitro antagonist potency and in vivo withdrawal precipitating potency are well correlated.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have shown that the quaternary derivative, QNXT, is a potent antagonist in vitro but not in vivo, and that this is due to the fact that the quaternized derivative does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
the quaternary derivative is not an effective opiate receptor antagonist in vivo.
